web_title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
book_title: Chapter 2: Inside Every Segment — Products, Customers & Real-World Examples
title: One Reported Segment, Four Product Lines, Two Different Businesses
question: What exactly does Xpro sell, to whom and at what economics, and how much of the profit comes from the specialty film versus the plain plastic sheet?

epigraph.quote: “Xpro is not - I would like to emphasize on the NOT, a packaging products company as we are often considered to be.”
epigraph.author: C. Bhaskar, Managing Director, Q4 FY2026 earnings call, 22 May 2026 [9]

web_blocks.html: Xpro reports one audited segment, “Polymers Processing”, in one geography, India (AR FY2026 note 44) [2]. Underneath sit three self-sufficient operating units that sell four product lines. The Biax unit at Barjora makes dielectric (capacitor) film. The Coex unit at Greater Noida and Ranjangaon makes coextruded sheets, thermoformed refrigerator liners and coextruded cast films [2]. A fifth leg, a UAE dielectric plant, is pre-revenue. On the audited product basis, Coex was 72.2% of FY2026 revenue (₹364.79 Cr of ₹505.49 Cr). Dielectric was 26.8% (our calculation) [2].

web_blocks.caption: Net sales by product line, ₹ Cr (audited product basis, net of inter-unit adjustments)
web_blocks.takeaway: Group revenue is flat over four years and the specialty line has shrunk 13.3% (our calculation). That is the opposite of the story the capex programme tells [2][23][21].

web_blocks.html: There are two small reconciliations. The FY2023 annual report showed Biax at ₹159.75 Cr on a divisional basis. The restated product basis used here shows ₹156.35 Cr [23][21]. Management’s calls cite Biax at about ₹141 Cr for FY2025 and a Coex:Biax mix moving from 75:25 to 71:29, against ₹136.34 Cr and a 25.5% dielectric share in the audit. We use the audited table [41][9].

web_blocks.caption: Tonnage, capacity, utilisation and realisation (our calculations from audited production and net sales)
web_blocks.takeaway: Sheet tonnage includes sheet consumed captively in forming, so sheet realisation looks too low and utilisation is an upper bound. The dielectric line has run near its ceiling for four years, and its realisation fell 11.0% (our calculation) [2][21].

web_blocks.html: H1 FY2027 is the first period with new capacity. Total production was 19,218 MT against 16,795 MT (+14%), and revenue was ₹351.1 Cr (+32.6%). In Q2 dielectric revenue grew 64% year on year, while sheets and cast films together grew 41% [3][14]. Sheet and liner volumes rose 18% in H1 and 26% in Q2 against refrigerator industry output up 4% in Q1 and 8% in Q2. Cast-film volumes were lower in H1 with a revival in Q2. Exports were ₹17.09 Cr against ₹9.39 Cr [3][14]. Divisional revenue and EBITDA for H1 are not disclosed.

This is polypropylene film, stretched on a stenter (a machine that pulls the film sideways while it is still hot) in an ultra-clean room. Thicknesses run from 3 to 15 micron, with 2 micron “under development” [14]. Variants include plain metallisable film in standard, high-temperature and “super grade” versions. There is also hazy film for oil-impregnated capacitors, with semi-rough grades for locomotive capacitors [14]. The customer base is narrow by design: “Our customer is only the capacitor industry” (Bhaskar, 22 May 2026). That means capacitor makers and film metallisers [9]. Dielectric sales are on letters of credit, “In the very, very specialized business, all sales are on LCs” [3].

Capacity is 4,000 MT at Barjora Line 1 plus 4,000 MT at Line 2 (commercial production declared 27 March 2026). The UAE line takes group nameplate to 13,000 MT [2]. Management quotes prices of about ₹470-480/kg for modal film, a little over ₹600/kg for 3.5 micron and near ₹900/kg for 3 micron (4 Nov 2026). These are premiums of 26% and 89% over ₹475 (our calculation) [3]. That compares with the audited average of ₹383/kg, which is 24% below ₹475 and is not reconciled by the company. The new line was “designed as a two-to-five-micron line”, so its tonnage depends on gauge [3]. Line 2 at 80% of 4,000 MT and ₹480/kg is ₹153.6 Cr a year (our calculation). That is within management’s ₹150-200 Cr per plant [41].

web_blocks.title: Worked example 1: a 3.5-micron film for an inverter capacitor

web_blocks.html: The customer. The customer is a film metalliser or capacitor maker. Filings name Super Electro Films, Dhruv Industries and Starion India, and Ind-Ra named TDK India [12][25]. Their buyers make EV inverters, solar and wind installations, grid equipment, railways and data centres (Xpro, 4 Nov 2026) [3]. The problem. Capacitor makers want thinner film for smaller capacitors. Ultra-thin film is hard to make and, “once the spec is changed … the supply has to be consistent” [3]. India imported roughly 70% of its base film in 2024 [42]. The product. The product is a 3.5 micron metallisable film, already approved by “some key customers” and priced at a little over ₹600/kg. One tonne is therefore about ₹6.0 lakh (our calculation) [3]. How it is made. Specialty capacitor-grade polypropylene granules are “not manufactured in India”. They are bought from global producers (Borouge is named) and held at three months’ stock. They are then extruded and stretched on a European stenter line under clean-room air, and slit [9][3]. How it is qualified, priced and delivered. Customers run capacitor life tests of 1,000 to 2,000 hours, and validation time can be “anything from zero to many months” [3]. Price is per kg with polymer cost passed through. Slit rolls ship direct, mostly to domestic customers, against a letter of credit [9]. Shipping container specifics are not disclosed.

web_blocks.takeaway: Most capacitor-film tonnage is still traditional, a segment forecast to grow only about 2.3% a year. The EV and renewables narrative therefore describes the growth, not the base [43].

web_blocks.html: That sizing uses Chinese industry data quoted in an IPO filing. It shows global demand of 136,000 t in 2024, EV and hybrid film of RMB 1.05 bn and inverter film of RMB 0.53 bn at RMB 70,000/t. That gives about 15,000 t of EV film and 7,571 t of China inverter film (our calculation) [43]. Xpro’s own application list (fans, coolers, ballast, power-factor correction) leans traditional. Its thin-gauge mix, not its tonnage, is what needs to change [14].

web_blocks.title: (b) and (c) Coextruded sheets and thermoformed refrigerator liners (Coex)

web_blocks.html: Coex melts ABS, polystyrene, polypropylene or polyethylene into sheets 0.2 to 7 mm thick and up to 2,300 mm wide. The sheets are plain or embossed, matt or gloss, and are supplied as roll, cut sheet or thermoformed parts [14]. Sheets plus liners were ₹310.09 Cr, 61.3% of FY2026 revenue [2]. Worked example 2. A refrigerator maker such as LG Electronics India (18% of FY2022 revenue per Ind-Ra), Haier, Godrej & Boyce, Voltas Beko or IFB buys inner cabinet and door liners [25][12]. The problem is cost and proximity. The OEM needs shaped liners in specified finish and polymer near its plant, at a tight price [14]. Xpro extrudes the sheet at Greater Noida (north India) or Ranjangaon (near Pune). It vacuum-forms the sheet on fully automatic lines with fast tool change and delivers direct to the assembly line [14]. Price follows polymer: “more or less directly related to crude” (Bhaskar, 30 May 2025), with Ind-Ra noting a minor lag [41][25]. Liners realise ₹269/kg against ₹105/kg for sheet (our calculation). Payment terms run to 120 days and debtor days were about 50 at March 2026 [2]. Liner weight per refrigerator and sheet gauge for liners are not disclosed. Sheet sales jumped 34.4% in FY2025 (production up 27.3%) as nameplate rose from 34,300 to 39,000 MT through lines bought from a competing manufacturer [21][45]. Sheet sales then fell 12.5% in FY2026 as tonnage dropped 6.5% (our calculation) [41]. The AR FY2026 also warns of “selective backward integration by certain customers, including under PLI-supported schemes” [2].

Two lines of 5,400 MT nameplate make polyethylene release film for the tyre, tread and conveyor-belt industry. They also make hygiene backing film for diapers, under-pads, sanitary napkins and surgical drapes, stretch wrap, and soft blister medical film [14][2]. Worked example 3. A tyre maker such as MRL Tyre or JK Tyre buys embossed or plain release film to keep uncured rubber layers from sticking. Its tonnage is small, at ₹54.70 Cr on 3,336 MT in FY2026 (₹164/kg, our calculation) [12][2]. Production fell 13.1% in FY2026 (3,841 to 3,336 MT, our calculation). The November 2026 release says cast films “continued to face competitive pressure”, and one line was revamped in 2026 for release films [6][14].

web_blocks.title: The fourth pillar: Xpro Dielectric Films, UAE

web_blocks.html: Xpro Dielectric Films FZ-LLC at Ras Al Khaimah is 85% owned since 12 December 2025 (Oasis II Investments Holdings took 15% for AED 33.09 mn). It is pre-revenue, with a FY2026 loss of ₹10.93 Cr [2]. Its first line is about 5,000 MT (13,000 less India’s 8,000; RAKEZ announced 4,500). The line is aimed at the USA, Europe and the Far East, on management’s point that the USA “does not manufacture base dielectric films” [35][41]. Equipment is installed, and dry runs begin December 2026 to January 2027, and commercial operation is expected later in FY2027 [3].

web_blocks.title: Profit by division: what is disclosed and what is implied

web_blocks.html: Because there is a single segment, profit share by division is not disclosed. Management’s ranges are dielectric EBITDA of 35% to 55% on conventional thicknesses and Coex of 5% to 7% (4 Nov 2026) [3]. Backing out the Coex range from audited standalone EBITDA gives a far lower implied dielectric margin.

web_blocks.caption: Implied dielectric EBITDA margin if Coex earns 5-7% (our calculation; ₹ Cr, standalone EBITDA before other income)
web_blocks.takeaway: At 35% on dielectric plus 5-7% on Coex, FY2026 EBITDA would have been ₹65.7-73.0 Cr against ₹49.2 Cr reported, a gap of 3.3-4.7% of revenue. At 55% the gap is 8.6-10.1% [2][3][16].

web_blocks.html: Our judgment. The Coex range is the more credible figure. It is a commodity-pass-through business, management has repeated it since 2024, and the arithmetic leaves little room for it to be wrong. The dielectric range is better read as a contribution margin on conventional gauges at peak pricing. It sits before shared overhead, FY2025 price cuts of 6-7% and build-up cost for Line 2 and the UAE team, which management cites among reasons for lower profit [41]. FY2024’s implied 30-34% was already below the “over 40%” management cited in May 2024. The fall to the high teens or low twenties by FY2025-FY2026 is the audited trail [38]. Our estimate of a fully loaded margin for the old line is roughly 20-30%. The new line’s Q1 FY2027 loss of about ₹7 Cr, improved by about ₹3 Cr in Q2, shows how large the drag is [3]. For scale, a scaled Chinese specialist reports a 46.6% gross margin in 2025, on a different cost basis [46].

web_blocks.takeaway: Placement Document and Ind-Ra naming covers some customers; Xpro’s own website shows unnamed logos [12][25][47].

web_blocks.html: One external customer was ₹149.41 Cr, 29.6% of FY2026 revenue (₹138.86 Cr, 25.9% in FY2025), and it is not named [2]. It exceeds all dielectric sales of ₹135.52 Cr, so it is most likely a refrigerator OEM, equal to 41.0% of Coex revenue (our calculation). That is our inference, not a disclosure [48]. The top 10 customers were 76.36% (FY2021), 71.72% (FY2022), 73.40% (FY2023) and 72.51% (9M FY2024) of gross revenue per the Placement Document. Ind-Ra put the figure at 75% for FY2022 [12][25]. Exports were ₹22.62 Cr in FY2022, ₹13.44 Cr in FY2024 and ₹22.45 Cr in FY2026 (4.44% of turnover). The destinations were USA and Germany for dielectric and Sri Lanka for sheets [2][21].

web_blocks.title: Two-sided read
paragraphs: Bull: the specialty film has real qualification barriers and customers who “want far more material than we have been able to supply” [49]. Coex is also gaining share, with volumes up 26% in Q2 against an industry up 8% [3].

Skeptic: the dielectric line has been flat for four years at about 3,550 MT, and its realisation fell 11.0% [14]. Customers’ qualification is not a lock-in on existing buyers while imports remain the larger share of the market. A 29.6% customer plus 5-7% Coex margins give the plain-plastic half of the group little pricing power [2].

book_paragraphs: Before we go any further, let me clear up the biggest misconception about this company. Most people hear “plastic film” and assume Xpro makes food packaging. Its managing director says otherwise, and he says it loudly: “Xpro is not - I would like to emphasize on the NOT, a packaging products company as we are often considered to be” [9]. What it makes, in fact, is two very different things under one roof, and you and I need to keep them apart in our heads. One is a specialty film that goes inside electrical capacitors. The other is plain plastic sheet that ends up as the inside wall of a refrigerator.

Here is the accounting wrinkle that shapes everything in this chapter. Xpro reports a single audited segment, which it calls Polymers Processing, in a single country, India [2]. That means the company never tells you how much profit each division makes. You get revenue by product, tonnes by product, and a few remarks from management on calls, and that is all. So the picture I am about to paint is part audited fact and part our own arithmetic, and I will tell you which is which as we go.

Start with revenue. In FY2026 the company sold ₹505.49 Cr of goods. The plain-plastic side, meaning coextruded sheets, refrigerator liners and cast films, was about 72% of that, and the specialty capacitor film was about 27% [2]. Now look at the four-year trend, because it surprised me. Total revenue is flat. The specialty film has shrunk by about 13% since FY2023, from ₹156.35 Cr to ₹135.52 Cr, while the plain plastic grew a little [2][23]. The expansion programme is built around the smaller, shrinking half of the business. Hold that thought.

Why did the film shrink? Not because customers walked away. Volume has stood almost still at about 3,550 tonnes for four years, because the one old line at Barjora is running near its ceiling at about 88% of its 4,000-tonne nameplate [2]. What fell was the price: from about ₹430 a kilogram of film in FY2023 to about ₹383 in FY2026, by my arithmetic. Management admits it cut prices by 6-7% on purpose, “in anticipation of the creation of new capacities” [41][9]. A company that cuts its own price when it cannot make more is protecting its customers before the competition shows up. Sensible, perhaps, but not what a price-setter does.

Now for the newest evidence. In the six months to September 2026, total production rose 14% and revenue rose 32.6% to ₹351.1 Cr, and in the second quarter capacitor-film revenue grew 64% from a year earlier while sheets and cast films together grew 41% [3][14]. Refrigerator sheet and liner volumes rose 18% for the half, against an industry up 4% in the first quarter and 8% in the second, and exports rose to ₹17.09 Cr from ₹9.39 Cr [3][14]. The company does not split the half by division, so we cannot see how much came from the new line. Here is a way to size it: if the second line runs at 80% of its 4,000 tonnes at ₹480 a kilogram, it is worth about ₹153.6 Cr a year by my arithmetic, within management’s own range of ₹150-200 Cr per plant [41].

Let me walk you through a real example, end to end. Imagine a company that makes capacitors for solar inverters. It does not buy raw plastic; it buys finished capacitor film, and Xpro tells us exactly who these buyers are: “Our customer is only the capacitor industry” [9]. Filings name Super Electro Films, Dhruv Industries and Starion India, and the rating agency has named TDK India [12][25]. This customer wants film that is thinner, because thinner film means a smaller capacitor, and a smaller capacitor means a lighter inverter. But it needs the same film every time. As management puts it, once the specification is changed, “the supply has to be consistent” [3].

So the customer orders a 3.5-micron film. A micron is a thousandth of a millimetre, so this is a sheet far thinner than a strand of hair. Management says this gauge is already approved by some key customers and sells for a little over ₹600 a kilogram [3]. That means one tonne is worth about ₹6 lakh. Compare that with the roughly ₹475 a kilogram for ordinary film and the ₹900 or so management quotes for 3-micron film, and you can see why the whole programme is a bet on getting thinner [3].

How is the film made? Specialty polypropylene granules, bought from global producers because the grades needed are “not manufactured in India”, are melted and extruded into a sheet [9]. The sheet is then stretched, including sideways on a machine called a stenter, a long oven with clips that pull the hot film wide, all inside a clean room. The big rolls are slit to the width the customer wants. And because the plastic is imported, the plant holds about three months of stock, which ties up cash [9][3].

Now the part that makes this a business and not just a factory: qualification. A capacitor maker cannot swap film suppliers casually, because the capacitor has to survive tests that run 1,000 to 2,000 hours, and the time to approve a film can be, in management’s words, “anything from zero to many months” [3][9]. Payment is secured too: “In the very, very specialized business, all sales are on LCs” [3]. An LC, or letter of credit, is a bank’s promise to pay. The rolls then ship direct to the customer, mostly within India, with no distributors in between. The company is explicit: “we are in a B2B segment” [41]. Exact container and logistics details are not disclosed.

Where does the capacitor go? Here is a point I want you to remember, because it is what separates the story from the base. Management says its films end up in EV inverters, solar and wind installations, grid equipment, railways and data centres [3]. All true. But Chinese industry data quoted in an IPO filing suggests EV and hybrid film is only about 11% of world capacitor-film tonnage, and inverter film for solar, wind and storage in China about 5.6% [43]. Fans, coolers, washing machines, air conditioners, lighting ballasts and power-factor equipment remain the bulk, and that traditional part is forecast to grow only about 2.3% a year [43]. The growth is real, but it is the smaller part.

Switch now to the other half. Picture a refrigerator factory, either near Delhi or near Pune. It needs the plastic liner for the inside of the cabinet and the door. Xpro makes the sheet at Greater Noida or Ranjangaon, vacuum-forms it into the shape on automatic lines, and delivers it to the assembly line [14]. Buyers named in filings include LG Electronics India, which the rating agency said was 18% of revenue in FY2022, Haier, Godrej & Boyce, Voltas Beko and IFB [25][12]. Sheets and liners together were about 61% of FY2026 revenue [2].

What about price? A kilogram of liner sells for about ₹269, and a kilogram of sheet for about ₹105, by my arithmetic, because sheet is partly consumed inside the plant to make the liner [2]. Management says these prices follow crude oil “more or less directly”, so when polymer costs move, the price follows with a small lag [41][25]. That is good for protecting the rupee margin and bad for growing it. Customers pay within about 120 days under the terms, and the company’s debtor days were about 50 at March 2026 [2]. The sheet side also has history: sales jumped about 34% in FY2025 after the company bought lines from a competitor, then fell about 12% in FY2026 [21][45][41]. And it warns of customers integrating backward and making their own sheet [2].

The last Coex line is cast film, made at Ranjangaon on two lines. One use is release film for tyre makers such as MRL Tyre and JK Tyre; it stops uncured rubber layers sticking together. Others are the backing for diapers and sanitary napkins, stretch wrap and medical blister film [14][12]. It is small: ₹54.70 Cr on 3,336 tonnes in FY2026, which is about ₹164 a kilogram [2]. Production fell about 13% that year, and the company says cast films “continued to face competitive pressure” [6]. One line has been revamped to focus on release film [14].

Now the fourth pillar, which has no revenue yet. In Ras Al Khaimah in the UAE, Xpro is finishing its first overseas plant through a subsidiary it now owns 85% of, after an Abu Dhabi investor took 15% [2]. The plant should add about 5,000 tonnes and is meant to sell to the United States, Europe and the Far East, since management says America does not manufacture base dielectric film [35][41]. Equipment is on site, dry runs start around December 2026, and commercial operation is expected later in the financial year [3].

Here is the question that matters most for you as an owner of this business: how much of the profit comes from the capacitor film? The company will not say. But we can do the arithmetic. Management says its capacitor film earns “between something like on the lower side 35% and going up to something like 55%” EBITDA, which means profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, and the plain-plastic side earns “in the 5% to 7% EBITDA range” [3]. Take the plain-plastic side at those margins and subtract it from the group’s audited EBITDA, and what is left for the capacitor film is a margin of about 30-35% in FY2024, 19-25% in FY2025 and 18-23% in FY2026 [2][16].

Run the test the other way. If the capacitor film really earned 35% and Coex 5-7%, FY2026 EBITDA would have been about ₹66-73 Cr. The company reported ₹49.2 Cr. At 55% the gap would be even wider [2]. So either the film margin is well below the quoted range, or something large sits unallocated. My judgment: the 5-7% on plain plastic is credible, because it is a pass-through business and the arithmetic leaves little room. The 35-55% is better read as a contribution margin on conventional gauges at good prices, before shared costs, the price cuts and the cost of staffing the new lines. In FY2024 the implied margin was already below the “over 40%” management had cited [38]. I would put the fully loaded margin on the old line at roughly 20-30%, an estimate and not a disclosure. The new line lost about ₹7 Cr in the June 2026 quarter, narrowing by about ₹3 Cr in the next one, which shows how big the drag has been [3].

Finally, concentration. One customer, which the company does not name, was 29.6% of FY2026 revenue, up from 25.9% in FY2025 [2]. That customer buys more than the entire capacitor-film business sells, so it is almost certainly a refrigerator maker, which I infer but cannot confirm. The top ten customers have been 72% to 76% of revenue in recent years [12]. Exports are small, ₹22.45 Cr in FY2026, or 4.44% of turnover, to the United States and Germany for dielectric film and to Sri Lanka for sheet [2].

Warren Buffett wrote that “a truly great business must have an enduring ‘moat’ that protects excellent returns on invested capital.” Xpro’s capacitor film has the beginnings of one: tests, approvals and a handful of imported-resin grades. Its plain-plastic half does not. The bull case is that customers “want far more material than we have been able to supply” and Coex is taking share, with volumes up 26% in the September 2026 quarter against an industry up 8% [49][3]. The skeptic’s case is that the film has been flat for four years, its price fell 11%, imports are still the larger share of the market, and a 29.6% customer on 5-7% margins gives little pricing power [14][2]. You can hold both views at once, and I would.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Two businesses share one name. One is a qualified specialty film whose true profit the company will not disclose; the other is a plain-plastic sheet business with thin margins and a very large customer. The audited numbers say the specialty half has not yet shown the earnings its quoted margin implies. The next test is whether thinner film, sold at a higher price from larger capacity, finally shows up in the reported profit.
